audits.title: gather information on the prudent use of antimicrobials in animals

recommendations.text: Authorisation, distribution and storage 16. In Germany, antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products are available only on prescription from a veterinarian and intended exclusively for use in the treatment of animals under the care of that veterinarian. BMEL informed the mission team that the rules on the prescribing and dispensing of such products by veterinarians are being actively discussed in Germany currently based on an opinion on veterinary dispensing law which concluded that the legal situation in this regard need not be amended. 17. In the case of food-producing animals, antibiotics can only be used by livestock holders following treatment instructions from a veterinarian and upon prescription. For food- producing animals the veterinarian can only dispense antibiotics which are not exclusively intended for local application to the livestock holder for 7 days, unless the authorisation conditions provide for a longer period of use (to avoid that livestock holders build up a stock of products without the veterinarian visiting the farm) whereas for other medicinal products available only on prescription this period is 31 days. The quantities of products dispensed and prescribed are required to be justifiable based on sound veterinary expertise, with the Federal drugs law and the Regulation on veterinary in-house pharmacies stating that the actions of veterinarians must be based on the current state of art of veterinary medicine. 18. A medicinal product may be used off-label in a therapeutic emergency pursuant to article 56a of the AMG. If a veterinary medicinal product is brought from another Member State or European Economic Area country in the event of a therapeutic emergency, it must be notified to the competent authority (pursuant to article 73 subpara. 3a of the AMG). No advance approval is issued by the competent authorities in such cases. Examples of recent off-label use communicated to the mission team included the introduction of a product containing doxycycline for use in cats in 2014 and 2015 and the use of a product containing bacitracin, neomycin and nystatin in dogs. Other examples included the use of products containing procaine benzylpenicillin and dihydrostreptomycin to treat horses. The mission team was informed by BVL that decisions on the import of a medicinal product from a non-EU country to treat animals in a therapeutic emergency lie within the decision-making competence of the Länder. 19. BVL informed the mission team that there is no monitoring programme for the off-label use of antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products in Germany. Checks on veterinary in- house pharmacies are performed nationwide by the individual Länder in accordance with a standardised checklist. The checklist seen by the mission team in the Land visited included questions such as: Does the veterinarian only prescribe and dispense veterinary medicinal products based on a sound diagnosis? Are there any microbiological results that would justify the choice of antibiotic? 5 Are medicinal products used/ repurposed only in accordance with the rules? 20. BVL was not aware of any other measures or initiatives going beyond the applicable national legislation for the purpose of restricting the off-label use of antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products. No central database exists to record any products used under special licence in animals (e.g. medicinal products intended for off-label use authorised for entry from another Member State or imported from a non-EU country). BVL stated that Länder authorities are responsible for this and BVL would only be contacted in an emergency situation for the provision of scientific advice. BVL stated that the use of human medicinal products by veterinarians would only be detected during inspections of veterinarians, and they could then be asked to justify their use.

Special conditions applicable to critically important antimicrobials 21. Concerning the referral outcome specified in Commission Decision C(2010)4684 of 1 July 2010 for veterinary medicinal products for food producing animals containing quinolones and/ or fluoroquinolones as active substances, BVL advised that there are no authorised products in Germany for which the product information has not yet been brought into line with this Commission Decision. The marketing authorisation holders for the veterinary medicinal products listed in Annex I to the Commission Decision have sent the updates to BVL in amendment notifications and in some cases the adjustments to the product information have been made as part of the renewal procedure. 22. Concerning the referral outcome specified in Commission Implementing Decision C(2012)182 of 13 January 2012 for veterinary medicinal products which contain the active substances cefquinome and ceftiofur, BVL advised that the marketing authorisation holders for the veterinary medicinal products listed in Annex I to the Implementing Decision have informed the BVL of the adjustments made to bring the product information into line with the Commission Decision in amendment notifications, and in some cases the adjustment has also been made as part of the renewal procedure. BVL advised the mission team that in Germany there is currently a veterinary medicinal product containing cefovecin. This preparation is authorised centrally, is intended exclusively for dogs and cats and therefore is not covered by the afore-mentioned Commission Decision. 23. Germany has guidelines for the prudent use of antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products (see section 4.3) which refer to the strict indication setting of 'antibiotic reserves' (in particular 3rd and 4th generation fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins). The guidelines state that these may be administered only under strict observation of the authorisation conditions, and only after a prior sensitivity check. For food-producing animals, the guidelines decree that the use of these antimicrobials should be reserved for the treatment of illnesses for which the administration of antimicrobials in other categories has shown, or is expected to show, little therapeutic effect. Since these are guidelines veterinarians are not legally obliged to follow them in practice, but are required to be able to justify their actions based on sound veterinary science. 6 24. As regards their authorisation and sales, there are currently no specific regulations or guidelines at national level for antimicrobials of particular significance for veterinary medicine (3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and macrolides according to the 2012 World Health Organization list of highest priority CIAs). In Germany, there are no particular antimicrobials whose use is explicitly prohibited in animals. 25. A key elements paper concerning regulatory provisions for the use of antimicrobials in animals has been published by BMEL to amend the Ordinance on veterinary in-house pharmacies (Tierärztliche Hausapotheken-Verordnung (TÄHAV)). Consultations on this paper, as well as discussions regarding possible future restrictions on the use of CIAs in animals, are ongoing. Financial incentives offered by pharmaceutical companies for the prescribing and purchasing of medicines (including antimicrobials) by veterinarians are also being discussed in the context of antibiotic resistance and keeping the use of antibiotics to a minimum. 26. BMEL informed the mission team that the various Länder and stakeholders have been consulted on this elements paper, with a hearing scheduled for mid-May and it is hoped to complete the process by the end of 2016. Possible new elements may include restricting off-label use of antibiotics in some species, making antibiograms compulsory for the use of some antibiotics etc. 27. BVL stated that a complete ban on the use of certain critical antimicrobials in veterinary medicine clashes with animal welfare concerns. They consider that sick animals should be treated with these active substances if no other appropriate treatment is possible. 28. BMEL expressed some thoughts on the recently published Commission guidelines on prudent use (see section 3), for example the recommendation that the prescription and use of CIAs "should be duly documented and justified" is not considered to offer sufficient guidance to Member States on how this should be achieved in practice, thus not facilitating a harmonised approach across the EU. The recommendation to only source animals from a single farm was also considered to present a difficulty for the financial viability of small farms which have an important societal value in Germany.

Monitoring and surveillance on the use of antimicrobials in animals 4.2.3.1 Use of antimicrobials in animals 29. Data on the volumes of veterinary medicinal products sold to veterinarians are entered into a database by wholesalers and retailers, based on the Verordnung über das datenbankgestützte Informationssystem über Arzneimittel (Regulation on the computerised medicinal product information system) of the German Institute for Medical Documentation and Information (Deutsche Institut für Medizinische Dokumentation und Information (DIMDI)). BVL publish a report based on these data, classified by region and individual substance classes. The volumes of products dispensed are categorised according to a number of geographic regions based on the first 7 two digits of the postal code of the veterinary in-house pharmacy. Therefore, although the total quantities of veterinary medicines (antibiotics) sold to all the veterinary practices in the area can be identified, individual practices cannot be identified for data protection reasons. The activities of some practices would also extend beyond Federal and State borders in some cases. Consequently, there is no direct link in this database between sales to veterinary practices and use of such veterinary medicinal products on holdings, although the overall flows of goods can be discerned. The mission team was informed by the Land authorities that since premixes are not included in the list of products in DIMDI, figures on their overall use in Germany are not available. 30. As part of the 16th amendment of the AMG applicable across Germany, a new system was introduced to compare medication use on fattening farms based on a benchmarking system. 31. This "antibiotic minimisation concept" and accompanying antibiotic database have been introduced as of July 2014 for turkey, broiler, pig and cattle farms (excluding laying hens, breeding turkeys, broiler parent and grandparent flocks, sows, pre-weaning piglets, suckling calves and dairy cows). Data on the total use of antibiotics during each six month period are entered by the farmer or an appointed third party, into the database. 32. The sources of the data are treatment records held on the farm, dispensing by the veterinarian, number of animals present on the farm at the start of the six month period in question and numbers of animal additions, removals, deaths etc. 33. Every six months a bi-annual holding treatment frequency is calculated for each farm based on the average number of animals held on the farm, number of animals treated, number of days a treatment is effective and number of antibiotic active substances administered during each treatment (despite concerns being expressed by some stakeholders on the data protection implications of such a database being developed). No higher weighting is given to any particular class of antimicrobials, such as CIAs. The mission team was informed that the quantity of medicine used is immaterial to the treatment frequency index calculation. A medicine containing three antibiotic active substances will be counted three times for the purpose of calculating the bi-annual holding treatment frequency. 34. The local competent authorities in individual Land calculate the treatment frequency per farm, based on the data submitted and a calculation methodology published in the Federal Gazette (number of treated animals multiplied by the number of days a treatment continues to be effective for each active substance in the medicine, divided by the average number of animals kept on the farm). These data are forwarded to BVL as anonymised information and relevant indicators for the whole of Germany are then calculated for the six month period in question (median and third quartile figures). 35. Data are classified in the following animal categories covered by the scheme: fattening turkeys, broilers, pigs under 30 kg, pigs over 30 kg, fattening cattle over 8 months and fattening cattle under 8 months. Small farms are excluded from the scheme: minimum 8 thresholds for the notification of data are 1 000 fattening turkeys, 10 000 broilers, 250 pigs under 30 kg, 250 pigs over 30 kg, 20 fattening cattle under 8 months and 20 fattening cattle over 8 months. A tolerance of plus or minus 5 kg is allowed in each weight category for pigs. 36. These data allow the monitoring authorities to assess the usage frequency for antimicrobials and compare farms against overall usage patterns. An individual authority can also only view the data on holdings which fall within its remit, not on holdings in other regions. 37. Within two months of the Federal data indicator being published, farmers are required to compare this national indicator with their own treatment frequency figure. If the farmer is above the median they should discuss the possible causes for this level of antibiotic use with their veterinarian. 38. Farmers in the top 25% of treatment frequencies are required to produce an action plan, normally in conjunction with their veterinarian, and submit this to the competent authorities on how the use of antibiotics on the farms could be decreased, for example through disease prevention, increased biosecurity and hygiene, use of diagnostics, antibiograms, vaccination, avoiding group treatments with antibiotics, improved feeding or reducing stocking density etc. (also making sure that any proposed decreased use of antimicrobials is not at the expense of animal health or welfare). No absolute targets for antibiotic use have been established, rather the use is benchmarked against other comparable farms. 39. The competent authorities receive the action plans and may assess them as part of risk- based monitoring. They may impose measures on the farm where necessary, for example to improve feeding, hygiene, reduce stocking density etc., to bring down the frequency of antibiotic treatments. The Land authorities advised the mission team that veterinarians had reported that this system of recording and obligation for action plans etc. had encouraged some farmers to accept the use of vaccinations on their farms, despite previous concerns regarding the costs of such vaccines. 40. For the Land visited by the mission team, it was found that the national median figures for cattle for fattening over and under 8 months of age for the 6 month period reviewed were zero, meaning that 50% of these farms reported zero antibiotic treatments for this period. The third quartile figure for cattle over 8 months was also zero, meaning that 75% of these farms reported zero treatments. Since this database was introduced there has been a trend towards decreased reported use of antibiotics and an increase in the number of farmers reporting zero treatments. 41. For a 6 month reporting period concluding 31 December 2015, by 14 January 2016 the figures on animal population and antibiotic usage should be entered into the database, by 28 February the Land should transmit the data to BVL, by 31 March the national indicators should be published, by 31 May individual farmers should have compared the data for their farm with the national indicators and produced (if required) by 31 July an 9 action plan on how to reduce antibiotic use on the farm. A corresponding cycle of data submission and reporting etc. occurs twice a year for each six month period. 42. A report on the operation of this scheme is required to be submitted to the German Parliament on 1 April 2019, in part to evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of the measures taken. 43. The Land authorities advised the mission team that the inclusion of dairy cows, or not, in this initiative had been a politically sensitive topic in Germany. They also expressed the concern that the administration of some antibiotic treatments might be brought forward to the pre-weaning stage for piglets or suckling stage for calves as these treatments would then not need to be recorded in the database. 44. Model or demonstration farms have been set up which farmers can visit or view online to identify good practices and increase their competence and awareness. 45. Under DART 2020 an internet-based management and database tool VetMAB has been developed which allows veterinarians to enter their own data on the use of antibiotics etc. and compare this with data from their peers. 46. BfR informed the mission team of various initiatives currently taking place under DART 2020 to record and assess the use of antibiotics and antimicrobial resistance monitoring, as well as epidemiological studies, research on the resistance of pathogens and its causes etc. 47. A research project VetCAb had considered the quantities and frequency of application of antibiotics administered or prescribed by participating veterinarians, and how to record the administration of medicines to farm animals on farm or in the dispensing veterinary practices. Building on these experiences, the VetCAb Sentinel research project is now keeping a constant record of the nature, quantity and frequency of antibiotic application, including the indications thereof, at a representative number of holdings. The therapeutic index can then be calculated (a different formula for the calculation is used in the antibiotic minimisation concept, and another therapeutic index is used by an industry quality assurance scheme QS (Qualität und Sicherheit: Quality and Safety for food). 48. A BVL-sponsored database VETIDATA developed by the University of Leipzig allows veterinarians to search through all authorised veterinary medicinal products by species, active substance, provides details of the underlying legislation etc., thus facilitating veterinarians in selecting an available product to be used and facilitating the more prudent use of antimicrobials. The mission team was informed that there are more than eight thousand registered users of this database. 49. An industry monitoring scheme QS covering inter alia the use of antibiotics in the pig and poultry sectors is also in operation. The mission team was informed that some data from this scheme, although shared with the competent authorities and veterinary organisations, is as yet unpublished and so considered confidential. 10 50. A number of antimicrobial resistance surveillance and monitoring programmes are in place in Germany, including monitoring in commensal germs, livestock pathogens and zoonotic pathogens based on EU legislation, with Germany also performing additional testing for MRSA, plasmid-mediated colistin resistance mechanism MCR-1 gene, ESBL etc. Monitoring is performed on farms, in slaughterhouses, at retail level and on imported food products. BfR informed the mission team that higher levels of ESBL are found in imported poultry meat and that 3.4% of all human MRSA isolates hint at a possible link to livestock. In the case of isolates from clinical cases, the figure is 2.6%. Conclusions on policies regarding the availability of antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products 51. Various schemes have been undertaken in Germany to monitor the use of antimicrobials in animals, including the antibiotic minimisation concept and accompanying database. Consideration is being given nationally as to whether further restrictions are necessary in the future on the availability and use of antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products, for example on CIAs which are also addressed in the existing prudent use guidelines. 4.3 POLICIES AND CONTROL ACTIONS ON THE USE OF ANTIMICROBIALS IN ANIMALS 52. Guidelines for the prudent use of antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products were first published in Germany in 2000, developed by the Federal Chamber of Veterinarians (Bundestierärztekammer) in cooperation with the Association of Chief Veterinary Officers (Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Leitenden Veterinärbeamten). These guidelines define the optimum approach to using antimicrobials in animals from the angle of veterinary medicine. In addition to the guidelines, annexes detail specific aspects relating to various animal species. 53. The guidelines are kept up to date and were revised in 2010 and again in January 2015. The current versions are published in the members' magazine of the German Veterinarians' Association (Deutsche Tierärzteschaft) and are regularly discussed at training courses for veterinarians. 54. The Federal Chamber of Veterinarians is an umbrella organisation of the chambers in all of the Länder in Germany, representing 39 000 veterinarians in Germany. Membership is compulsory for veterinarians and the chamber's central bureau represents official veterinarians, practising veterinarians and those working in veterinary science. 55. Committees within the chamber work on issues such as veterinary medicinal products and feed, have been involved in the development of the afore-mentioned prudent use guidelines and the antibiotic minimisation concept etc. Current work topics include the use of colistin in animals and possible new regulations being discussed in Germany (see section 4.2.2). The chamber collaborates with the Federal Chamber of Human Medical Doctors on matters of common interest such as antimicrobial resistance and prudent use. The chamber also highlighted to the mission team a current issue concerning the 11 availability of penicillins, which need to be imported from abroad owing to supply difficulties with a German manufacturer and that veterinarians may have to resort to using cephalosporins due to penicillins not being available. 56. Information was also provided on an academy for veterinary training (Akademie für tierärztliche Fortbildung (ATF)) which is a subsidiary of the chamber. audits.title: Animal Welfare - Transport

recommendations.text: To correct the current system for approving vehicles for transport of bovine animals so that the suitability of the vehicles' drinking systems for different categories of bovines (weaned versus unweaned calves), required by Annex I, Chapter VI, point 2.2 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, is identifiable from the vehicle approval certificates. rd bullet.

citations.text: The Animal Welfare Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe fur Tierschutz) of the working groups for Consumer Health Protection (Landerarbeitsgemeinschaft Verbraucherschutz Arbeitsgruppen) is the major driver in the development of inter-Länder documented procedures for official controls on animal welfare. The presidency rotates according to the selection of a new presidency Land, with the Federal level invited to the working group meetings.

Regarding the vehicle's conditions: The stocking density (Annex I, Chapter III, point 2.1 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005) is checked during the administrative checks, and verified during loading; Local competent authorities generally require a technical opinion from vehicle test engineers from semi-private accredited vehicle inspection and certification bodies and, taking into account the specialised technical knowledge required this is considered a good practice. In the two Länder visited all local CAs except one, followed this procedure. BVL confirmed that the local authorities in some other Länder inspect and approve vehicles without this specialised technical opinion. When renewing the 5-year approval (Article18 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005) the full range of checks carried out for a new vehicle approval is also performed; Neither of the Länder visited had issued vehicle approval certificates with a distinction between categories of bovine animals (e.g. Adult cattle, weaned/unweaned calves). Approval certificates state simply "Bovine animals" without indicating if the vehicles are appropriate for unweaned calves. Therefore unweaned calves may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animal, with the biggest risk being their inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Annex I, Chapter VI, point 2.2 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005); However, one of the Länder visited provided evidence of making that distinction between categories of pigs (approval certificate was for `pigs and piglets'); The main section of the Handbook about vehicle approval also does not refer to unweaned calves. One annex to the Handbook does explicitly mention unweaned 7 calves in connection with approval while this distinction is not made in the Handbook template for the vehicle certificate.

The current system for certification of approved vehicles does not sufficiently distinguish the types of vehicle appropriate for different categories of bovine animals. As a result unweaned calves may be transported in vehicles with unsuitable drinking devices and may not have access to liquid nor be fed, if necessary, during long distance journeys.

recommendations.text: To ensure that contingency plans of transporters exporting live animals include measures to meet the animals' needs for bedding, feed and water in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at the border as required by Articles 3(a) and 11(1)(b)(iv) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

citations.text: Contingency plans set up by transporters do not include adequate measures to provide bedding, feed and water to the animals in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at the border and the competent authorities do not require for that to be included. There are, therefore, inadequate assurances that the needs of animals blocked at the border can be met and that these animals are not caused unnecessary suffering.

recommendations.text: To ensure that feed business operators meet the requirements on hazard analysis and critical control points' (HACCP) system in accordance with Article 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and that the competent authorities ensure the effectiveness of official controls in this regard, as required by Article 4(2(a)) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: At every establishment visited, the audit team checked the assessment of the operators' HACCP-plans by the feed inspectors. In many cases, the inspectors' assessment was sufficient. However, at six of 11 establishments visited, the audit team noted shortcomings in relation to adequacy of risk assessment for some ingredients used for the production of feed additives and for hazards which may arise during certain processing steps (predominantly contaminants of chemical origin, e.g., heavy metals, dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), etc.). The failure of the operators to identify relevant hazards, as requested by Article 6(2(a)) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, was neither spotted by the inspectors met during the audit nor had these issues been identified in the previous inspection reports. In one case there was no feed additive- related HACCP-plan. This was correctly spotted by the inspector met but was not described in the reports from the three previous inspections of this facility (carried out by other inspectors). Absence of permanent written procedure(s) based on the HACCP principles is not in line with the requirements laid down by Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. The effectiveness of the inspections, in terms of completeness of the operators' record-keeping and appropriateness of the retained samples, can be further enhanced by focused and comprehensive checks of traceability. There are opportunities for improvement in the assessment of the operators' HACCP-plans. The verification of the correctness of labelling is normally not a part of the routine inspections, which reduces the competent authorities' possibility to adequately verify that labelling requirements have been met by FeBOs. 6 In its response to the draft report the competent authority noted that point 3.2 of the feed control programme stipulates that the inspection must cover, inter alia, checking/examination of labelling, packaging and advertising. 8 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that the official controls include verification that feed business operators' meet their obligations on traceability, especially in terms of completeness of the operators' record-keeping and appropriateness of the samples taken, as required by Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 10(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and sections on "Record-keeping" and "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: The audit team observed that the examination of (ingredient/product) traceability is not included in every inspection, this was confirmed by the competent authorities in the Länder visited.

In general, the feed inspectors met showed good theoretical knowledge on the relevant legislative provisions laid down by Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Nonetheless, at five establishments of 11 visited, traceability was inhibited by deficient record-keeping by the operators (absence of unique identification (batch number) for incoming ingredients, several identification numbers created for the same product during processing, identical identification numbers given to different final products, absence of system to unambiguously distinguish between different batches of the same ingredient in a continuous process). Such deficient record-keeping resulted in inadequate reconciliation of the documentation provided during the traceability exercises. In particular, information on the number of the batch or of the specific portion of production, in the case of continuous manufacture, was not always provided by the operators, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in the section on "Record-keeping"(2(b)(i)) in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. These shortcomings were rarely spotted by the inspectors met during the audit, nor had they been reflected in the previous inspection reports.

As for the operators' obligation to take samples of ingredients and of each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market or of each specific portion of production (in the case of continuous production) in sufficient quantity using a procedure pre-established by the manufacturer (hereinafter: retained samples), the audit team observed several samples in all of the establishments visited and noted that in many cases they could not be considered as adequate due to the absence of a pre- established written procedure (on taking of retained samples) by the operators, absence of sealing, and/or insufficient quantity. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by part "Quality control"(4) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Only the absence of the sealing was spotted by the majority of the inspectors met during the audit but only once had this been reflected as a non-compliance in the previous inspection reports examined by the audit team.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. The effectiveness of the inspections, in terms of completeness of the operators' record-keeping and appropriateness of the retained samples, can be further enhanced by focused and comprehensive checks of traceability. There are opportunities for improvement in the assessment of the operators' HACCP-plans. The verification of the correctness of labelling is normally not a part of the routine inspections, which reduces the competent authorities' possibility to adequately verify that labelling requirements have been met by FeBOs. 6 In its response to the draft report the competent authority noted that point 3.2 of the feed control programme stipulates that the inspection must cover, inter alia, checking/examination of labelling, packaging and advertising. 8 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: Ensure that meticulous plant health checks can be, and are, carried out on a representative sample of each consignment of regulated plants and plant products, so as to ensure that plants, plant products and other objects are not contaminated by harmful organisms, as required by Article 13(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC. to 92.

citations.text: However, the samples applied in the majority of cases at Frankfurt Airport are significantly smaller than those suggested in ISPM 31 to achieve the level of reliability set out in the Compendium, and necessary to reasonably conclude that the plants and 19 plant products are not contaminated with harmful organisms, as required by Article 13(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The import checks in Germany are carried out meticulously, in line with either national or local guidelines. The effectiveness of the plant health checks carried out at the two main points of entry for plants and plant products is compromised though, by the size of the samples taken for 'non-ISPM 31' checks at Frankfurt Airport, which significantly reduce the probability of detecting any harmful organisms that are present, and the reduced checks of regulated commodities at peak times, at Hamburg port, which is not in line with EU legislation.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the inspection guidelines available to the responsible official bodies are up-to-date, in line with Article 1 and Item 1(a) of the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC.

citations.text: The LPPS also issue guidance for performing import checks, which is more tailored to the trade at individual points of entry. This includes formal guidance, issued by the LPPS itself, as well as informal guidance, shared between inspectors to assist in interpreting import requirements and legislation, or the Compendium. During visits to the points of entry, the audit team noted that: Sampling guidance had been issued for performing checks of low-risk commodities ('non-ISPM 31' checks ­ see section 5.4.4 below) at Frankfurt airport, which differed significantly to that established in the Compendium, and ISPM 31; Guidance on EU import requirements was being used by inspectors at one point of entry. This was developed locally, based on guidance developed by another point of entry. Both guidelines were undated and did not include recent changes in EU legislation and import requirements.

Inspectors have access to instructions and guidelines for import controls, in line with Article 1, and Item 1(a) of the Annex, to Directive 98/22/EC. However, the local guidance for inspection and national legislation maintained at some points of entry were not up-to-date, as required by that same legislation.
This is however undermined by the resources available for performing checks at the key points of entry and the use of locally issued guidelines that are not up-to-date.

audits.title: Animal welfare - quality controls and indicators

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should ensure that the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources for animal welfare reflect the strategic objectives of the Multi-annual National Control Plan (MANCP) as required in Article 42 (2) (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The setting of strategic and operational objectives should take into consideration the guidance provided in the MANCP network reference document "Developing Objectives and Indicators" developed by the MANCP network.

citations.text: The Länder working group on animal welfare (LAV-AGT) has identified seven general strategic and operational objectives for the areas of food and feed safety, animal health and welfare. The first relates to optimising the quality management system (QMS) for official controls across all competent authorities and sectors including verification through appropriate audit systems. This should, by default, improve consistency and efficacy of controls, i.e. have an impact on animal welfare. However, there is no baseline set or operational objectives laid down to measure if projected outcomes for animal welfare are successful or not.

The second and third "strategic" objectives relate to improving procedures and are, as such, operational rather than strategic objectives. There is no link between the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect these objectives. Article 42 (2) (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect the strategic objectives of the MANCP.

In addition, these are not measureable objectives on what Germany wants to achieve for animal welfare. There are no specific strategic objectives indicated in relation to animal welfare outcomes e.g. reduce incidence of tail docking by x%, improve FPD levels by x%, decrease lameness levels in cattle by x % through official controls and related actions in the MANCP such as training, targeted enforcement campaigns on certain issues, liaison with sector to set agreed targets etc. For instance, considering the amount of resources devoted to the development and drafting of an Action Plan on tail docking of pigs there is no mention of it as either a strategic or an operational objective (with measureable targets) in the MANCP nor any meaningful reporting on its implementation in either the annual report on the MANCP, or in the report to the Commission on official controls on farms required by Commission Decision 2006/778.

Documentation related to the Action Plan on tail docking of pigs is included in the QMS documentation of the Land (Federal State) visited but only for information purposes. The Action Plan on tail docking of pigs is not included as a clear objective identified for 4 Article 42 (2) (a) The MANCP network reference document "Developing Objectives and Indicators" states that the underlying principle behind these requirements and guidelines is that we cannot manage our control systems without setting clear objectives and monitoring progress towards those objectives. A strategic objective is a long-term objective, setting out what an official control system and its priorities intend to achieve. Strategic objectives usually relate to outcomes and impacts. Objectives should be Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-bound (SMART). 3 official controls and does not form part of the Manual of animal welfare monitoring in livestock holdings (hereafter the Handbook).

The competent authorities' approach to the setting of objectives and the planning and reporting of official controls is mainly operational "business as usual" with no targets, indicators or measurement of progress, nor any prioritisation of controls or allocation of resources and as such is insufficient to bring measureable change.

Previously there had been animal welfare objectives set in the Land visited, such as, on group housing of sows where the local level (Kreis - district or county) were asked to carry out specific controls. However, currently as there is no legal spur for such a focus, there are no specific objectives set for animal welfare controls at Land level, nor were any specific reports received at Land level on local level objectives or activities.

citations.text: The annual report on the MANCP gives statistics on compliance for each of the areas covered by Decision 2006/778 and Article 27 of Regulation 1/2005. Nonetheless, it does not indicate whether the actions taken are contributing to improvements, whether compliance/detection is improving/decreasing and whether the activities are suitable to reach the objectives and ensure effective operation of the MANCP, including enforcement action and its results as required under Article 44 (1) (d) of Regulation EC No 882/2004.

There are output indicators such as the quantity of inspections and non-compliances detected per inspection but these do not give an outcome for animal welfare. The outputs are not linked to the existing strategic objectives.

The reports sent to the Commission by Germany on Decision 2006/778 give only a collation of non-compliances with no analysis at any level of the significance of the findings or the root causes or any influencing factors. Article 8 of the Decision requires an analysis of the most serious findings of non-compliance and a national action plan to prevent or decrease their occurrence for the forthcoming years. The reports merely list essentially the same findings and actions to address them each year.

For example an extract from the German 2006/778 report for 2018 indicated: Free Barn Enriched Unenriched Calves Pigs range cage cage 6,108 67,223 Holdings subject to inspection 8,002 840 147 0 101,844 5,129 867 Inspected holdings 78 0 6,541 818 Production sites without non- 747 65 0 5,110 3.521 compliance These inspections resulted in the following enforcement action being taken: Non-compliance A 46 100 15 0 2,266 2,702 Non-compliance B 0 112 271 Non-compliance C 4 16 1 0 389 470 2 15 1 There is no analysis available on why the inspections on pig or calf farms resulted in much higher rates of non-compliance detected on farm (31% pigs, 22% calves) than on barn holdings for laying hens (11%) for instance, or why there were much higher percentages of serious non-compliances in category C for these species or what these issues were and what can and should be done to address them.

There is potentially useful data within this framework but the reporting is not reliable in certain cases or analysed to any degree e.g. mutilations on pigs were reported as 99% compliant, although this is not the case as approximately 95% pigs are routinely tail docked. The guidance for inspectors on this issue relates to whether the mutilation was carried out correctly and does not question whether the mutilation should have been carried out in the first place according to the legislative requirements in Point 8 of Annex I, Chapter I to Directive 2008/120/EC.

The Land level authority knew very little about the type of issues or their significance reported from the local level to them under Commission Decision 2006/778 as neither they nor the local level had analysed the results of inspections reported from local level before sending on the information to BMEL. The lack of Land level knowledge on the outcome of controls was noted in previous Directorate F audits (DG SANTE report 2018-6445 on pigs).

There is no specific report on broilers produced as required in Article 7(2) of Directive 2007/43/EC. Data on inspections on these farms was available in the Land visited, but there is no aggregated report for the whole country and no analysis of the non- 7 compliances generated. The revised Official Control Regulation (EU) 2017/625 gives the opportunity to report on these inspections within a defined format from 2021 onwards.

The Annual Report on implementation of the MANCP and the report on animal welfare required under Commission Decision 2006/778 give at best a superficial analysis of the results of official controls on animal welfare. Official control results are simply reported in terms of compliance/non-compliance.

There is insufficient analysis on the results of controls to enable authorities at different levels to have a clear picture of the animal welfare situation on farm and to assist them in developing strategies to address the major issues.

audits.title: Processed animal proteins

recommendations.text: To put measures in place to ensure the accuracy of the lists of food and animal by- product establishments eligible to supply animal by-products and produce processed animal protein to be used for aquaculture as laid down in Section A, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

citations.text: Listing of food establishments authorised to deliver raw materials for production of non- ruminant PAP and ABP, and feed operators authorised to produce feed materials and compound feed with PAP for aquaculture animals, is a federal responsibility. Each Land has to communicate the list of these establishments to the federal level. These lists are available on the BMEL website. The audit team identified that in Bavaria several food establishment (slaughterhouses, cutting plants) slaughtering and/or cutting bovine and porcine animals were listed. The competent authorities stated that some of these establishments had not provided evidence of having an effective system in place to prevent cross-contamination between ruminant and non-ruminant by-products contrary the requirements of point (a), Section D, Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and listing of these food establishments is a result of a miscommunication. Representatives of the competent authorities stated during the final meeting that they will propose the de-listing of these establishments soon. In Lower-Saxony, one 5 slaughterhouse slaughtering bovine and porcine animals was listed. The audit team assessed this authorisation and it was in line with the above-mentioned legal requirements.

The processing plant visited delivered poultry PAP for feed production for aquaculture animals. This processing plant was not listed on the BMEL website contrary to the requirements of point 1(d), Section A, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 While this processing plant was subject to regular official controls, the competent authority has not detected this non-compliance.

recommendations.text: To put measures in place to ensure that record-keeping and microbiological sampling of the 30 days validation of processing method 7 is in line with the requirements of point G, Chapter III, Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: Three processing plants visited were using processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant during the 30 days validation period microbiological samples were taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) directly after the treatment. This is not in line with the legal requirements for the testing of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae in PAP. The problem was identified by the competent authority and the sampling was repeated for Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae two weeks later. During the repeated sampling the operator increased the minimum temperature in the drier and reduced the speed of the conveyor screw which may increase the safety of the produced product. However, the processing method before and after the requested modification were different, resulting in different process parameters during the 30-day validation period. This is not in line with the requirements of point G, Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The competent authority overlooked this requirement during the approval of the validation.

In another processing plant visited using method 7, during the 30 days validation period samples were taken for microbiological controls (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae and Clostridium perfringens). However, for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae only one sample of each were taken contrary the requirements of point G 1(c) (ii) of Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The competent authority did not note this problem and approved the validation of the processing method. In the third processing plant visited using method 7 the validation documents were comprehensive and complete as required by the legislation. 2 In its response to the draft report the competent authority noted: The establishment concerned provides its staff with regular training on the state of raw materials, contamination with impurities and correct categorisation. Establishments supplying category 3 materials are also required to make a statement, in which the producer of category 3 material declares, among other things, that the material is free from digestive tract content. In the wake of the finding, the competent authority increased the frequency of inspection of the material supplied and the associated own-checks by the establishment. 9

Official inspections on operators' HACCP systems are carried out adequately, however problems identified regarding official validation of processing method 7 and official sampling weaken the effectiveness of these controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official sampling, including collection, analyses and communication of results is in line with the requirements of Chapter I, Annex X, to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: Two of the four processing plants visited were located in Bavaria. In one plant, official samples for microbiological analyses were not taken between 2011 and 2018 because the competent authority stated they did not identify in this plant any relevant problem during official controls that would require official sampling (see finding 19). In 2018, two samples were taken for Salmonella detection from PAP as feed material by the feed control authority. Non-compliance was not detected in these samples. In the other plant visited, official microbiological samples were taken for the verification of the heat treatment in 2018. Microbiological contamination was not detected in these samples, however the results of the official laboratory for Enterobacteriaceae was reported as "Not detected in 25 grams", instead of in 1 gram, contrary the requirements of Chapter I, Annex X, of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

In two processing plants visited located in Lower-Saxony, official microbiological samples were taken for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae from PAP. However, in several cases the number of samples sent for laboratory tests was lower than that required by Chapter I, Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

In all processing plants visited, regular microbiological samples were taken by operators for microbiological control of produced PAP. In one plant, samples were always taken from the production line not from the storage of final product; in another plant, only 1-1 samples were taken from each production batch for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae. While these plants were subject to official inspections, the local inspectors had not identified that such sampling is not in line with the requirements of Chapter I, Annex X, of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

Official inspections on operators' HACCP systems are carried out adequately, however problems identified regarding official validation of processing method 7 and official sampling weaken the effectiveness of these controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that information about the arrival of consignments of processed animal protein is notified to the Member State of origin, by means of TRACES, as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: A number of guides are available to support the use of TRACES: - The FLI has prepared a guidance document with the most important questions and answers relating to the use of TRACES and a general instruction on the use of the DOCOM (commercial document) part of TRACES in case of trade in Category 1, 2 and 3 ABP and derived products. - In Bavaria, chapter 13.2 of the ABP manual gives detailed instructions on the use of TRACES in case of intra-EU trade of PAP including the obligatory notification back to the place of origin. Chapter 14.3 gives detailed instructions on the use of TRACES in case of export of PAP containing ruminant protein. There is no instruction on the requirement for TRACES notifications in case of intra-EU trade of OF/SI, however. - The training materials developed by Lower-Saxony (see finding 8) to support the technical use of TRACES are available on the website of the LAVES. 5.1.4 Conclusions on the system of official controls

The audit team noted that, although guidance/instructions (see finding 22) were established to this effect by the competent authorities, arrivals of consignments of PAP were not systematically confirmed by the German competent authorities to the competent authorities of the Member State of origin by means of TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017 and in 2018, around 23% and 30%, respectively, of such arrivals were not notified back.

Inadequate checks on the implementation of requirements concerning confirmation of TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI negatively affect the reliability of the flow of information on the intra-EU trade of such products.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the arrival of consignments of processed animal protein containing ruminant proteins intended for export is confirmed at the point of exit from the EU and any seal checks carried out are recorded in TRACES, and that the competent authority responsible for carrying out official controls at the establishment from which the consignment originates, verifies the correct implementation of the applicable requirements of channelling procedure and checks whether the confirmation of the seal check carried out at the point of exit on each consignment of processed animal protein derived from ruminants that is intended for export is recorded, as required by Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

citations.text: The audit team visited a paper trader (see finding 10). The trader started its business in 2008 and it was registered based on Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 in December 2016. In 2018, the arrival to the BIP of approximately 10% of the export consignments containing PAP with ruminant protein traded by the operator was not confirmed in TRACES and no information was available on the seal check, contrary to the requirements of Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Local official controls had not detected this problem during the last official inspection in January 2019. The audit team reviewed the documentation provided by the operator (invoice, bill of loading) proving that these consignments had arrived at the port indicated in TRACES. 5.2.2 Requirements for identification and traceability of PAP produced and traded to and from other Member States

The audit team identified several systematic shortcomings relating to TRACES notifications of consignments containing ruminant PAP intended for export from Germany to third countries and to the official controls in this regard: 11 Contrary to the requirements of fourth sentence of point 1(c) of Section E, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, the arrival of significant numbers of consignments intended for export at the point of exit notified in TRACES was not confirmed by the relevant BIP in Germany. In cases where the consignments were intended for export via another Member State and the authorities of the exit point did not confirm the arrival of these consignments at their BIPs, the German competent authority had not sought confirmation of arrival from the authorities in that other Member State to satisfy itself that the German establishment under its control complied with the obligation of notification of the arrival of the consignment at the place of exit and that the consignment has actually arrived to that destination. Records of seal checks at BIPs (in Germany and in other Member States) were not available in TRACES in relation to a significant number of consignments originating in Germany, making it difficult for the relevant competent authorities to demonstrate that these checks have actually taken place. Contrary to the requirements of point 1(d) of Section E, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, in processing plants visited exporting PAP containing ruminant protein to third countries, the competent authorities did not carry out official controls to verify that confirmation relating to the arrival of the export consignments to the point of exit was received through TRACES. Several consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein were incorrectly declared as being for technical use in TRACES. The competent authority explained during the audit that some of these consignments were not presented for seal checks at the BIPs because the producer was not aware of this legal requirement and accordingly these consignments had not been subjected to the channelling procedure applicable to consignments containing ruminant PAP intended for export. In several cases the operators declared designated points of entry as the points of exit in TRACES for export of consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein, contrary to the requirements of point 1(a) of Section E, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. This non-compliance was not detected by the competent authorities. In several cases consignments intended for export arrived to another BIP, not the one which was notified in TRACES by the operator. This was not followed up by the competent authorities. Pre-notifications (see findings 43 and 44) containing information about the container numbers, seal numbers, date of arrival to the BIP were not systematically sent to the BIP notified in TRACES as the point of exit. And this was not followed up on by the competent authorities. In conclusion, the channelling requirements for export of consignments containing ruminant PAP are not always implemented in Germany in compliance with the requirements of Section E, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. 12

Significant numbers of consignments of PAP which did not contain ruminant proteins were notified in TRACES (as "Mammalia-Ruminantia") although such consignments are not subject to official control in this regard at the point of exit. In several cases consignments produced in processing plants which are not approved for production of PAP containing ruminant protein (for example processing plants with only pig PAP processing lines) declared the species as Mammalia. These inconsistent declarations of the goods (animal species) in TRACES by the business operators created confusion at the points of exit, because based on the TRACES notification it was not clear to the relevant authorities whether it was required to confirm the arrival of these consignments and to carry out and record the seal check.

In 2018, 14 Category 3 export consignments were notified in TRACES as Category 1 and Category 2 products. The competent authority had identified these mistakes although the TRACES notifications were only corrected during the audit.

Considering the high number of missing confirmations on the arrival of consignments containing ruminant PAP from points of exit in Germany and in other Member States and the lack of control mechanisms in PAP processing plants to verify that the confirmation of the seal check at the point of exit had been received through TRACES, the German competent authorities could not always ensure that the channelling 14 procedure for export of PAP containing ruminant protein is adequately implemented.

citations.text: The analytical procedure and validation data for beta-agonists (A5) in liver by LC- MS/MS (41) and for antibiotics (B1, multiresidue method) in red and white muscle were reviewed (42). The method was validated prior to the introduction of the current EURL guidance, however, for some substances, chlorbrombuterol, clenproperol, isoxuprine and carbuterol, the CC values were above the recommended concentrations set out in the 2007 EURL guidance document (44). In response to this finding, the laboratory noted that carbuterol is not a mandatory substance for the national control plan in Germany and indicated that the substances showed poor sensitivity at lower levels on the instrument used at the time of the validation. In addition, assurances were provided by the TLV laboratory that the method will be revalidated by 2022 in line with the MMPR values. The NRL also indicated the intention that the methods in official laboratories in Germany will reflect the MMPR guidance levels by 2022. b. Further to point a. above, the laboratory stated that in the case of prohibited or non-authorised substances with pharmacological action, a non-compliance (39) Order on the Establishment of the State Office for Consumer Protection of 27 November 2012, GVBl.2012, 478, https://landesrecht.thueringen.de/bsth/document/jlr-LAVerbrSchErAnOTHrahmen. (40) Thuringia Food Monitoring Act, ThürlMÜG, of 8 July 2009, GVBl.2009, 581, section 1 and 2, https://landesrecht.thueringen.de/bsth/document/jlr-LM%C3%9CbGTH2009V6P1. (41) BA-90-003-1, Determination of beta-agonists in liver with LC-MS/MS. (42) AB-01-001-1, Determination of antibiotics in muscle of red white meat using LC-MS/MS. This approach is not exactly in line with the EU requirements, i.e. the result of an analysis shall be considered non-compliant where it is equal to or above the decision limit for confirmation (CC) (45). c. in the case of antibiotics (B1), the CC values were determined only at a single maximum residue limit (MRL) level for substances where MRLs vary based on species. audits.title: Official controls on feed hygiene

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are consistently implemented to allow for adequate assessment of feed business operators' HACCP systems.

citations.text: In the majority of the feed establishments visited, the audit team assessed the HACCP system and in particular the assessment of hazard analyses by the competent authorities. In three cases, the local inspectors carried out comprehensive inspections on the HACCP in the two months preceding the audit; no HACCP-related non-compliances were identified. In one of the three cases, the assessment of the hazard analyses by the local inspector was adequate. However, in two other cases, the audit team noted that the hazard analyses were incomplete (e.g. hazards related to raw materials and ingredients used were not part of the hazard analysis). This is not in line with the requirement of Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. This deficiency was overlooked during previous official inspections.

In one establishment visited, the FeBO identified a critical control point (CCP) in its own hazard analysis. However, the audit team noted that the established critical limit and monitoring procedure were not adequate for this CCP. Additionally, the hazard analyses of this establishment was very general (e.g. several hazards relating to incoming raw materials were not assessed). This is not in line with the requirement of Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. These deficiencies were overlooked during previous official inspections.

In two compound feed producers visited, the local inspectors carried out comprehensive HACCP inspection. However, in one establishment visited, the audit team noted that the competent authority's assessment of the operator's tests on homogeneity of mixing and carry-over of coccidiostats were superficial, and that the inspectors experienced difficulties to interpret the testing procedures and results. In another establishment visited, the local inspector made an adequate assessment of the company's documentation both for mixing homogeneity and for carry-over of coccidiostats. The working group (see finding 3) prepared a guidance document on this topic (see finding 14); the audit team noted that local inspectors in one Land visited used this guidance.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. Official inspections were generally well performed, allowing for adequate verification of operators' fulfilment of the relevant legislative requirements, in particular on feed hygiene, maintenance of equipment and traceability. However, weaknesses in the assessment of operators' HACCP systems and shortcomings in labelling controls weaken the effectiveness of the control system. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling 30. Planning of official sampling is described in the report DG(SANTE) 2018-6315 (see point 4 and footnote 1). In short, the BMEL, in cooperation with the BVL, the Federal Institute for Risk Assessment and the Länder, prepares a five-year programme the animal feed control programme including the planning of the official feed sampling. The sampling plan includes undesirable substances as referred to in Directive 2002/32/EC, pesticide residues as referred to in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005, unauthorised substances (e.g. veterinary medicinal products and prohibited animal proteins), prohibited materials as referred to in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009, genetically modified organisms, etc. Sampling covers the whole feed chain, i.e. both primary and non-primary FeBOs.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators' labelling satisfies the pertinent legal requirements.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and Articles 15 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009.

citations.text: In both Länder visited, assessment of feed labels was a part of the inspections. In general, labels were collected and assessed during official sampling, or during comprehensive controls. There were adequate guidance/checklists to support the assessment of the labels by feed inspectors. The audit team examined a number of inspection records and noted that, in most cases, the local inspectors did not identify any labelling deficiencies (only in a few cases were some inaccuracies reported). The audit team re-assessed the content of labels previously checked by the inspectors and noted that some of the labels, considered correct during the official controls, were in fact deficient, namely: · The feeding instruction on the label of a complementary feed for cattle for fattening would result in an enzyme concentration (in complete feed) lower than the minimum established by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1059/2013; · On some complementary feed labels, there were no dosage instructions at all. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 17(1)(b) of, and point 4 of Annex II to, Regulation (EC) No 767/2009; · One label of a feed additive did not contain information on the maximum content for different animal species, which had been established by relevant authorisation legal act. This is not in line with the requirements of by Article 16(1)(e) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. 7

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. Official inspections were generally well performed, allowing for adequate verification of operators' fulfilment of the relevant legislative requirements, in particular on feed hygiene, maintenance of equipment and traceability. However, weaknesses in the assessment of operators' HACCP systems and shortcomings in labelling controls weaken the effectiveness of the control system. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling 30. Planning of official sampling is described in the report DG(SANTE) 2018-6315 (see point 4 and footnote 1). In short, the BMEL, in cooperation with the BVL, the Federal Institute for Risk Assessment and the Länder, prepares a five-year programme the animal feed control programme including the planning of the official feed sampling. The sampling plan includes undesirable substances as referred to in Directive 2002/32/EC, pesticide residues as referred to in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005, unauthorised substances (e.g. veterinary medicinal products and prohibited animal proteins), prohibited materials as referred to in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009, genetically modified organisms, etc. Sampling covers the whole feed chain, i.e. both primary and non-primary FeBOs.

audits.title: Import controls for plant health

recommendations.text: Ensure that documented control procedures for conducting official controls are developed in accordance with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and updated following the requirement of Article 12(3)(b) of the same Regulation.

citations.text: The JKI and the Länder are working on a Quality Management System for plant health, which will include working instructions. The development in the LPPS is ongoing and the JKI informed the audit team that Bremen has issued a quality management manual. 4 In their response to the draft report, the Competent Authorities noted that the lifting of the ePhyto procedure in Hamburg is planned for early 2022. After that, consignments of wood packaging will be cleared via TRACES. 11

Standard operating procedures (SOP) are currently being developed by the LPPS and are technically commented on by the JKI. They will be made available in the Compendium according to the information provided by the JKI.

Out of the three LPPS interviewed during the audit, only NRW has in place SOPs for import control of fruits and cut flowers and a written procedure to approve BCPs and CPs. In the other Länder, development of the SOPs is at different stages. According to the information provided by the JKI, from the other Länder only Bremen has developed SOPs.
The JKI informed the audit team that many LPPS including Hamburg, NRW and Saxony- Anhalt follow the guidance for sampling of consignments provided in the Compendium for plant health checks.
Brandenburg, Baden-Wuerttemberg and Bavaria report to have developed their own guidelines based on the units and requirements listed in Annex III to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

Hesse reported that sampling procedures are not yet adapted to Annex III to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130, as the implementation has shown to be complicated. The effects of not updating the sampling procedures are described in point 5.3.3, when inspectors at Frankfurt airport BCP determine the size of the inspection sample to conduct physical checks. 5.2.3 Frequency of checks

Documented control procedures have not been timely updated to reflect the legal requirements, so the CAs cannot ensure that official controls of plants, plant products and other objects are carried out effectively, preventing the possible introduction of pests in the EU territory5.

The designation and re-designation of BCPs, CPs and other inspection facilities is done by the LPPS under Articles 59 (1), (2) and (5), Article 61, Article 62 (1) and (2), Article 63 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The BMEL and JKI stated that they do not coordinate on this issue from federal level. a) NRW provided the audit team with a SOP used to ensure designation and re- designation of BCPs and CPs in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2017/625 and Implementing Regulation 2019/1014. 19 b) In Hamburg and Hessen, the LPPSs stated that they do not have any procedure to ensure that BCPs and CPs comply with the requirements of the above EU Regulations. c) In addition, in Hamburg port BCP, the CA stated that the commercial storage facilities have not undergone any checks to ensure that the minimum requirements of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 were met.

recommendations.text: Ensure that competent authorities have control verification procedures in place in accordance with Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The JKI informed that an ad hoc group was established in 2005 with six senior officers from the LPPS, one expert from the JKI and another expert from the BMEL, in order to plan internal audits on plant health controls. The usual audit team consists of two members of the LPPS, one JKI staff and another member of the BMEL who take this as an additional task and report to the BMEL, Land Ministries and the LPPS. The aim is to conduct one or two audits per year on different subjects, including import, export, plant passport, etc. Over the past years and as stated by the JKI, audits have focussed on monitoring and plant passports. Since 2013, two audits related to plant health import controls were conducted at federal level, one at Hamburg in 2013 and another at Berlin in 20181. This audit team assessed the report of the audit conducted in 2018, which covered, among other elements, implementation of Directive 2000/29/EC. The JKI informed the audit team that at Land level, internal audits have been carried out only in those Länder, which have already implemented a quality management system. This point was verified in the interviews conducted with the LPPS.

The CAs at Federal level and in the three Länder covered, Hamburg, Hesse and NRW, stated that they have no control verification activities on plant health import controls in place, contrary to the requirements of Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The consequences of this are described in point 5.3.3. 5.1.4 Planning of official controls

The absence of control verification procedures in place undermines the capability of the CAs to identify outdated documented procedures and take corrective actions in the cases where shortcomings are detected.

The audit team was shown three videos together with photographs of inspectors carrying out identity and physical checks on various types of consignments at Hamburg seaport BCP, Frankfurt airport BCP and a CP in NRW. Statements made by the CAs reinforced the information provided in these videos and photographs. The audit team made the following observations: a) In Frankfurt airport BCP, during the demonstration of physical checks of basil stems (Ocimum sp.), in order to create the inspection sample, the inspector selected from the boxes bunches of herbs in sufficient numbers to meet the minimum requirements established in the EU Regulation. However, while conducting the visual check of the stems to verify the absence of harmful organisms under the magnifying glass, as the bundles were not untied and only the exterior stems were checked, the inspector did not inspect a sufficient number of them to identify with 95 % reliability a level of 5 % or above of infested plants, in accordance with the requirements of point 4(d) of Annex III to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. When questioned about the existence of written guidelines on how to conduct inspections, the inspector stated that there were no written instructions available to the inspectors on how to conduct inspections (see paragraph 44). b) At the same BCP in Hesse, during the simulated inspection demonstration of a mixed fruit consignment, the inspector informed the audit team about the fruits which would be physically inspected and those that would not, based on the reduced frequency system applied at this BCP. However, although the inspector indicated the need to check a defined number of boxes for each type of fruit present in the consignment (five), it was stated that only the fruits in the upper part of the box would be checked, without defining the minimum number of units to be checked for each lot in the consignment. Consequently, she could not identify the minimum inspection sample size needed in order to detect the presence of a harmful organism in accordance with the requirements of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130 (see paragraph 44). Therefore, the audit team could not identify a systematic approach to determine the size of the inspection sample and achieve the requirements of point 4(d) of Annex III to the above Regulation. 17 c) During the video demonstration at the CP in the Straelen area of NRW, the inspector selected Rosa sp. stems taken from a delivery covered by six different phytosanitary certificates. To build the inspection sample, these stems were selected in numbers proportional to the presence of each variety in the delivery, not taking into consideration the units covered by each phytosanitary certificate separately. This meant that, for the varieties with lower presence in the consignment, the physical inspection did not achieve the minimum requirements of point 4(d) of Annex III to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. This was because the consignment for inspection was not properly identified as the quantity of goods covered by the same official certificate, as defined by point (37) of Article 3 of Regulation 2017/6256. Consequently, it cannot guarantee an appropriate level of phytosanitary protection, as well as, an effective overview on the imports of plants and plant products into the Union and the risks thereof.
