audits.title: Import controls

recommendations.text: To ensure that the staff who may assist the official veterinarian in the performance of physical checks or perform physical checks have successfully completed a training programme, which complies with the requirements of Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1081.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 49(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1081

citations.text: The audit team noted however, that the competent authorities of one Land did not provide evidence that staff authorised to assist the official veterinarian in carrying out physical checks or to carry out physical checks had successfully completed a training programme that meets the requirements of Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1081. 5.1.4 Documented procedures and arrangements in place

However, the fact that some documented procedures and arrangements are not up-to-date and a training programme for staff assisting the official veterinarians in the conduct of their controls has not been fully established, and the absence of sufficient verification that the monitoring plan has been implemented, may undermine the overall effectiveness of official controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are performed in accordance with documented procedures and arrangements which have been updated as appropriate.

citations.text: The LAV AG ED has issued a `Manual for Border Inspection Posts', last revised in 2015, which provides guidance on official controls of animals and products of animal origin entering the EU through German BCPs. This manual has been drawn up by the LAV AG ED to support the performance of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU. The competent authorities stated that due to the ongoing amendments to national legislation on official controls the manual is not up-to-date, which is not in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the OCR.

The audit team noted that in addition to the `Manual for Border Inspection Posts', all Länder authorities have documented control procedures in place. Whereas four Länder have procedures updated as appropriate, the remaining five did not, which is not in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the same Regulation. One specific example noted by the audit team was that at one BCP not all of the arrangements which are required by Article 64(3)(d) and (e) of the OCR are in place (see also section 5.3).

However, the fact that some documented procedures and arrangements are not up-to-date and a training programme for staff assisting the official veterinarians in the conduct of their controls has not been fully established, and the absence of sufficient verification that the monitoring plan has been implemented, may undermine the overall effectiveness of official controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

The audit team noted that in the case of BCP Berlin-Brandenburg airport, based on the information provided by the competent authorities, there are no facilities for unloading, inspection and storage of the categories of products of non-animal origin not intended for human consumption for which the BCP is designated, which is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The audit team further noted that the unloading area for categories of animals is shared with categories of goods of animal origin not intended for human consumption, which is not in line with Article 5(5) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In addition, the audit team noted that not all of the arrangements which are required by Article 64(3)(d) and (e) of the OCR are in place.

None of the BCPs evaluated are fully compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for one or more of the categories of animals and goods for which they have been designated. Consequently the competent authorities cannot guarantee the appropriate handling of animals and goods, the proper verification of compliance of those animals and goods and the prevention of the risk of cross contamination in these facilities. 16

recommendations.text: To ensure that consignments containing goods derived from more than one consignment of origin or product categories, transported from approved warehouses to a vessel leaving the EU where the consignments are intended for ship supplying purposes, are accompanied with an official certificate in accordance with the model set out in the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128.

citations.text: For two deliveries of several consignments of goods of animal origin to vessels leaving the Union where the consignments were intended for ship supplying purposes, the BCP staff issued in each case a single official certificate. Both deliveries were acknowledged at destination. The official certificates issued were not in accordance with the model certificate set out in the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128, which is not in line with 29(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. The audit team noted that certificates issued referred to repealed legislation, and did not mention the reference numbers of the CHEDs for the consignments from which the products were derived.

However, a number of shortcomings were noted in the implementation of official controls which concerned, for example, prior notification, controls on consignments transported from approved warehouses to a vessel leaving the EU where the consignments are intended for ship supplying purposes, and decisions taken on consignments. These shortcomings 14 however did not significantly undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods entering the EU.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the BCP staff take a decision on each consignment of animals and goods following the performance of official controls, indicating whether the consignment is in compliance with the rules referred to in Article 1(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and record the outcome of said controls and any decision taken on that basis in Part II of the CHED.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 55(1) and 56(3)(b) and 56(5)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 40(2)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715

citations.text: In the case of a consignment of captive birds introduced and to be followed by a period of quarantine before import, the audit team noted that, in Part II of the CHED, the consignment was indicated as acceptable for the internal market rather than for quarantine, and the details of the quarantine establishment were not indicated, which is not in line with Articles 55(1) and 56(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 40(2)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715.

The audit team also noted that the impact of the transport on animals was not completed in Part II of six out of the ten CHED-As evaluated, which is not in line with Article 56(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 40(2)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715.

The audit team identified two CHED-Ps finalised in TRACES-NT for the same consignment. The first CHED contained a decision to refuse entry of the consignment and indicated re-dispatch outside the EU. Following a request of the operator to authorise the consignment for transit to a third country, a second CHED for the consignment was finalised without cancelling and replacing the original CHED. The audit team noted that, as a consequence, two different decisions have been recorded in TRACES-NT on the same consignment, which is not in line with Article 55(1) and 56(5)(c) of the OCR.

However, a number of shortcomings were noted in the implementation of official controls which concerned, for example, prior notification, controls on consignments transported from approved warehouses to a vessel leaving the EU where the consignments are intended for ship supplying purposes, and decisions taken on consignments. These shortcomings 14 however did not significantly undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods entering the EU.

recommendations.text: To ensure that designated border control posts comply with the minimum requirements for border control posts appropriate for the categories of animals and goods for which the post has been designated, including the commercial storage facilities which may be used for identity and physical checks on products of non-animal origin.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 64(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3, 4 and 5 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014

citations.text: The audit team noted that the BCP Bremerhaven has no storage facilities for chilled and frozen categories of products of non-animal origin for which it is designated, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In addition, the competent authorities informed the audit team that, in exceptional cases, it permits physical checks on consignments of products of non-animal origin to be carried out at commercial storage facilities. However, the audit team noted that those facilities did not have the required inspection rooms or areas, which is not in line with Article 3(11) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The competent authorities informed the audit team that the BCPs Frankfurt airport and Leipzig Halle airport did not have housing areas or rooms to separately detain the registered equidae and ungulates other than registered equidae, the categories of animals of which are included in the scope of designation for both BCPs, which is not in line with the requirements of Article 5(1)(e)(i) and (ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The authorities stated that there is a time separation between the handling and housing of both categories of animals, with cleaning and disinfection carried out during the period of time separation. Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 does not provide the possibility to derogate from the requirement to have housing facilities to separately detain categories of animals.

The audit team noted that in the case of BCP Berlin-Brandenburg airport, based on the information provided by the competent authorities, there are no facilities for unloading, inspection and storage of the categories of products of non-animal origin not intended for human consumption for which the BCP is designated, which is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The audit team further noted that the unloading area for categories of animals is shared with categories of goods of animal origin not intended for human consumption, which is not in line with Article 5(5) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In addition, the audit team noted that not all of the arrangements which are required by Article 64(3)(d) and (e) of the OCR are in place.

citations.text: The CCA informed the audit team that all over Germany, regular official controls in the FNAO chain, regarding microbiological risks, take place after harvest. All Länder have introduced IT programmes/tools for the management of official controls. All sampling and control data collected are, in principle, recorded in the IT system.

Saxony-Anhalt informed the audit team that the official controls started to be carried out before and during the harvest as of May 2023, when the established control frequencies were technically implemented (integrated into the IT system). A project group is in the process of developing the ensuing detailed checklist and specific instructions. 6

Bavaria stated that inspections before and during harvest are requested by the Land Ministry but cannot be carried out due to staff shortages. Inspections pre- and during harvest, are carried out in case of specific campaigns or outbreaks. For outbreak situations, specific instructions and checklists are available from LGL.

In the farms visited, regular inspections took place after harvest, at the level of premises (packing area, buildings and facilities) and the inspection frequency was largely respected. The generic checklist was used. Non-compliances were identified and recorded in the reports, which were mainly related to structural shortcomings. However, evidence of follow-up activities was not provided, despite clear instructions from the regional CAs that follow-up of non-compliances should be reported.

In the second visit, official control was performed without a checklist and was limited to the premises. The inspector informed the audit team that he does not carry out official controls before and during harvest.

audits.title: Collect information on the national system to protect fish welfare in aquaculture

recommendations.text: Research and emerging technologies Findings 19. One of the research institutes met during the remote part of the study is working in partnership with a university on a project (NatiMon) to collect indicators and parameters for determining animal welfare in rainbow trout and carp farms.: · This project aims at creating the basis for a regular and harmonised indicator-based animal welfare monitoring for key aquaculture species. · The identified welfare indicators are ­ preliminarily ­ mortality, dissolved oxygen levels, morphological conditions of the fish (e.g. skin or eye problems, fin or body lesions) and swimming behaviour. · The project is expected to be completed in 2023 and will result in the publication of guidance brochures ­ one for carp and one for trout ­ to assist stakeholders in identifying, measuring and assessing the welfare indicators on the aquaculture farm. · The project will not establish ranges or limits to determine satisfactory levels of welfare in the farms. 20. One of the associations met during the remote part of the study published a guidance document `Animal welfare indicators' to assist fish farmers in the practical implementation of their own checks. This document provides indicative water quality parameters to be met for salmonid and carp welfare, and possible corrective measures that 7 can be taken to address related issues. However, none of the farmers met during the on-the-spot part of the study were measuring these parameters. 21. Research and competent authority representatives agreed that dissolved oxygen is the most important water quality parameter to monitor for fish welfare. 22. The long-distance transporter visited during the on-the-spot part of the study had collaborated to a project (Fish Transport Project ­ FiT) aimed at developing a mobile fish transport system with integrated water treatment. The system developed significantly reduces the carbon dioxide concentration in the water thus improving water quality and fish welfare during transport.

Quality assurance schemes and fish farmers' own checks Findings 23. In their reply to the pre-mission questionnaire, the competent authorities did not identify any quality scheme specifically promoting the welfare of farmed fish. 24. Qualified veterinary services visit farms on a regular basis due to animal health EU requirements. One of these services ­ met during the on-the-spot visits to the fish aquaculture farms ­ can measure oxygen saturation and temperature levels in the water for fish health reasons.: · These parameters could also serve as animal welfare indicators. Currently they do not record the general morphological conditions of the fish (mortalities, skin or eye problems, fin or body lesions). · This qualified service is drafting a protocol ­ based on the results of the NatiMon project ­ to record lesions that would indicate animal welfare or animal health issues and to check other animal welfare indicators. 25. Fish farmers met during the on-the-spot part of the study indicated that the main welfare indicator they assess is mortality but that they would record this only when it exceeds normal daily mortality. Article 186(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on transmissible animal diseases requires the farms visited to keep mortality records in any case. · Farmers rearing the same fish species in similar conditions each gave a significantly different value to "normal daily mortality". · Only one of the farms visited kept mortality records, including the numbers and total weight of dead fish. This is considered a good practice, as it provides an idea of the production stage of the fish concerned. · The other farmers had empty mortality records although there had been disease outbreaks in their farms. In one case, the farmer had recently requested the intervention of the Fish Health Service because of high mortalities throughout a full week but had not recorded these in the mortality sheet. 8 26. Stakeholders met during the remote part of the study indicated that monitoring and measuring animal welfare indicators becomes increasingly relevant with increasing intensity and technology of the farming system. 27. Operators transporting fish (mainly on short journeys) identify oxygen saturation as the critical water quality factor to ensure fish welfare during transport. 28. Farmers are generally stunning the fish using a percussive blow to the head before bleeding them. 5.3 CHALLENGES FACED 29. Fish farmers met during the on-the-spot part of the study indicated that their main welfare concern is the prevention of predators as these kill and injure the fish they are keeping. 30. The stakeholders met during the study and a representative from one of the States' competent authorities indicated that they would disagree with establishing generic limits for most welfare parameters since these limits would vary depending on the production systems, fish species and their life stages. 31. The representative of one of the producers' associations met during the remote part of the study indicated that there is limited access to private veterinarians specialised in aquaculture health and production. This is causing delays in obtaining timely diagnoses and, consequently, longer waiting times to provide suitable treatment to the fish. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Germany has set up a system for official controls on the welfare of farmed fish. There are advisory documented procedures supporting the official controls on fish farms. National legislation in Germany requires fish farmers to measure and assess animal welfare indicators on their farms. However, there are generally no clearly defined limits for welfare indicators at farm in documented procedures nor in most guidance available. The exceptions are a recently developed documented procedure in one of the States visited and a guidance document produced by an association. This guidance provides indicative water quality parameters for salmonids and carp but fish farmers do not seem to be using it. Their welfare indicator of preference is mortality but in general farmers are not recording this, making it difficult for competent authorities to assess farms' own checks. Additionally, there is ongoing research to provide stakeholders with indicators and parameters for determining animal welfare in rainbow trout and carp farms. This would help fish farmers in managing fish welfare in their farms. German transporters consider dissolved oxygen levels in the water as the critical welfare indicator during transport. This is generally the only parameter they monitor and is done indirectly through the flow rate of oxygen pumped into the water. However, there is ongoing 9 research to control other water quality parameters during the journey, such as dissolved carbon dioxide. Currently, the fish aquaculture representatives would not want EU legislation on fish welfare that is not species, and production system, specific. The impact of predators is the main welfare concern to fish famers. 7 CLOSING MEETING The study team held a closing meeting on 31 May 2023 with representatives from the federal level and from the states visited, at which the main findings of the fact-finding study were presented.

recommendations.text: Ensure that inspectors have access to sufficiently detailed instructions as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to ensure the effectiveness, quality 2. and consistency of official controls on authorised operators as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Ensure that the competent authorities have access to a sufficient number of staff in line with Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in order to comply with Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, in particular Article 92(1) which requires that all authorised operators are subject to at least one official control per year.

citations.text: At Federal level, there are procedures in place to ensure the effectiveness, quality and consistency of official controls as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The compendium of phytosanitary controls provides general information on all areas of the plant health system, including basic work instructions and procedures. In the context of plant passports, it contains instructions for registering operators and checklists for conducting controls on authorised operators. Both Länder visited had developed detailed templates for conducting controls based on the templates in the compendium. However, they had not developed sufficiently detailed instructions for inspectors as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to ensure the effectiveness, quality and consistency of official controls on authorised operators as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and as described in paragraph 31.

The failure to conduct official controls with the required frequency and the lack of sufficiently detailed instructions for inspectors negatively impacts on the effectiveness, quality and consistency of official controls on authorised operators.

While these checklists address all legal requirements of authorised operators, the controls observed by the audit team did not verify if authorised operators comply with relevant requirements outlined in paragraph 21 as required by Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. This was due to insufficiently detailed instructions for inspectors as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (paragraph 5), with the result that inspectors did not perform high quality controls effectively and consistently, as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The consistent failure to conduct the legally required minimum number of official controls, coupled with the superficial nature of these controls provides limited assurances that authorised operators fully meet the requirements for issuing plant passports.

The checklist used by inspectors when conducting official controls at authorised operators includes a question on traceability. However, due to the lack of clear guidance for inspectors as described in paragraph 31, these controls do not systematically check if authorised operators have traceability systems within and between their premises as required by Article 70 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 15 5.6.2 Official controls on sales through distance contracts

Weaknesses in the system of official controls means that it is not ensured that there are adequate traceability systems in place for plants subject to plant passports, except in the case of cultures subject to certification requirements.

audits.title: Authorisation and controls of marketing and use of Plant Protection Products

recommendations.text: To ensure that controls of PPP operators in the chain of marketing and use of PPPs, including PPP manufacturers/re-packers, are performed following a risk-based frequency as required by Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In the Länder visited, representatives of the CAs stated that operators in the chain of marketing and use of PPPs are subject to a variable frequency of inspections based on the afore mentioned federal control priorities, specific Land legislation (where relevant) and the knowledge and experience of the local authorities. In one of the two main Länder visited by the audit team, the annual plan of controls includes a fixed number of traders (retailers, wholesalers and online traders) to be inspected (around 20% of the 15 total number), in the other one, traders selling exclusively to non-professional users (e.g. garden centres) are inspected annually. The large traders selling only to professional users are also inspected annually, while smaller external storage sites and traders are inspected every two years. The audit team noted that among the criteria used to determine the frequency of inspections of these operators, certain criteria related to the individual operators such as, the outcome of previous official controls and the reliability and results of own controls performed by the operator or by a third party, were not considered. This is not in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In this regard, it should be noted that the AG-PMK has recently drawn up a comprehensive procedure to score PPP operators based on objective risk criteria, which aims to harmonise the frequency of inspections of PPP operators. Nonetheless, representatives from the CAs of the Länder visited stated that this procedure is not yet implementable due to some delays in developing the necessary database.

At federal level, the working group AG-PMK plays an important role in recommending measures to plan official controls across Germany in a coordinated, harmonised and risk-based way. National control priorities are determined annually and a procedure to score PPPs operators based on objective risk criteria was recently drawn up. While the national control priorities are generally considered by the Länder during their planning, the frequencies of inspection of various PPP operators have so far not been determined by objective risk criteria. This weakness, which can cause heterogeneous levels of controls across Germany, could be addressed by implementing the afore-mentioned procedure. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

In Germany, there are around 60 PPP manufacturers (including re-packers), and the audit team noted that, by the time of the audit, only 11 of them had been inspected to verify they comply fully with the applicable requirements. These inspections were performed by inspectors from the relevant Land supported by experts from the BVL. Representatives from the CAs stated that the applicable control criteria have only been recently developed at federal level and may require further review (see finding 34) and that the delay in implementing controls was mainly due to the limited expertise of the Länder inspectors in this type of PPP operator. The audit team noted that, given the potential risk posed by these PPP operators, the frequency of inspection so far has not been in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (see also finding 43).

The system of official controls at import and of PPP traders is implemented in a coordinated manner, according to the risk-based control priorities agreed at national level and by sufficiently knowledgeable inspectors from the Länder who, generally, follow the control methods laid down in the national control manual. This represents a solid and harmonised basis to ensure that only authorised PPPs are placed on the national market. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of system is partly weakened by the fact that a limited number of controls of PPP manufacturers have been carried out, so far, and insufficient attention has been paid to ensure that PPPs not authorised in Germany are actually exported. recommendations.text: To put in place inspection requirements to ensure that unauthorised PPPs intended for export are actually exported from Germany, as laid down by Article 28(2)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

citations.text: The audit team visited a PPP operator carrying out manufacturing activities on behalf of various PPP authorisation holders. This manufacturer had not been inspected previously by the CA from the relevant Land and was only visited in 2020 to take a sample. The inspection observed by the audit team, which was carried out by inspectors from the relevant Land and a representative from BVL, was comprehensive. Nonetheless, the audit team noted that the CAs were not aware that the manufacturer was exporting PPPs not authorised in Germany from this plant and that no checks were carried out to ensure that such PPPs were actually exported to the place of destination, which is not in line with Article 28(2)(d) of Regulation (EC) 1107/2009. It was confirmed that no specific measures are in place in the Länder visited nor at federal level, to ensure that such PPPs are not used in Germany11.

The system of official controls at import and of PPP traders is implemented in a coordinated manner, according to the risk-based control priorities agreed at national level and by sufficiently knowledgeable inspectors from the Länder who, generally, follow the control methods laid down in the national control manual. This represents a solid and harmonised basis to ensure that only authorised PPPs are placed on the national market. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of system is partly weakened by the fact that a limited number of controls of PPP manufacturers have been carried out, so far, and insufficient attention has been paid to ensure that PPPs not authorised in Germany are actually exported. audits.title: Production and placing on the market of meat preparations and meat products

recommendations.text: To comply with Article 18(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the CAs need to enhance the effectiveness of official controls aimed at verifying that FBOs fulfil their obligations, as specified in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. This includes, but is not limited to, verifying that FBOs, applying arrangements based on national guides to good hygiene practices, have adequate procedures based on HACCP principles to effectively manage microbiological risks related to ready-to-eat meat products.

citations.text: The audit team noted in all the establishments visited that they were approved for all the activities carried out. However, in the two small capacity establishments visited it was noted that: · when flexibility arrangements were applied, this was not specified in any document (e.g. the approval licence or in the establishment profile), and · when the audit team requested the HACCP plans contained in the approval file of the establishments, a copy of the Guidelines on good hygiene practices for artisanal butchers was presented (see paragraphs 2 and 4). It was noted that the FBOs had not adapted the HACCP plans of the Guidelines to the specific activities/production they carry out nor had identified the relevant parts applicable to their businesses (see paragraph 41). Thus, the approval was given without an assessment of the suitability of the HACCP plan and its coverage of the hazards to the specific products.

Specific procedures for the approval of food business establishments are in place, enabling the CAs to maintain oversight and take appropriate actions when the conditions are no longer met. While these approval procedures are generally well-executed, implementation in small capacity establishments reveals shortcomings that compromise the effectiveness of official controls, notably in terms of the adequacy of HACCP plans to address hazards related to particular production processes. 7

In the two small capacity meat products/meat preparation establishments visited the CAs explained that the FBOs were implementing the HACCP plans provided in the "Guidelines on good hygiene practices for artisanal butchers". However, as outlined in paragraph 27, the specific risks associated with particular products/processes had not been identified, thus leaving uncertainty about the measures to be taken to mitigate those risks. Furthermore, FBOs had not conducted characterization of different RTE products, making it unclear if they could support Listeria monocytogenes growth, which is not in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. In one of these establishments, approved since 2019, the CA requested the FBO, a month prior to this audit, to analyse their products (salami) for pH and water activity (aw) to justify the FBO`s decision that the product does not support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes (see also paragraph 49). The laboratory results were not yet available at the time of the audit team's visit.

In one small capacity establishment visited the FBO conducted annual tests on one RTE product (one sample unit) in an accredited laboratory, including tests for Listeria monocytogenes. The audit team examined the laboratory results which noted that "the 10 sample was tested according to the specification of the German Butchers` Association". The limit set for Listeria monocytogenes was 100 cfu/g for this RTE product able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes (point 1.2 of Chapter 1 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005). However, there was no study available to support that this limit is not exceeded at the end of the shelf-life of the product.

However, these controls are not effective to identify the systemic non-compliances in small-scale food business in relation to the arrangements regarding the design and implementation of FBOs' procedures based on HACCP principles. In addition, in the medium/large-scale food businesses there are some weaknesses in CAs' assessment of the adequacy of HACCP plans and, in particular, of FBOs' own check sampling plans.

recommendations.text: In order to comply with Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, the CAs should improve the effectiveness of official controls aimed at verifying that FBOs' own-check sampling programmes comply with the sampling plans laid down in Chapters 1 and 2 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

citations.text: The audit team noted in one of the three establishments visited (in one of the Länder) producing RTE meat products that the OVs responsible for the official controls were not familiar with some areas (e.g. the applicable microbiological criteria for Listeria monocytogenes) (see also paragraph 47). These OVs, who are also responsible for official controls in establishments producing other commodities (e.g. dairy, fishery products) had not received specific training on RTE products. This failure to keep the knowledge of staff 5 conducting official controls up to date is not in line with Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. According to the BVL representative, they are veterinarians and, based on their training, should have the knowledge to carry out controls on different areas. 5.2.2 Supervision of CA staff and audits

A training system designed to ensure that official personnel can carry out their tasks effectively is established, with official control staff having access to expert groups in various fields for support. However, specific training on certain subjects relevant to the sector audited has not been conducted thus far. This gap could account for the weaknesses the audit team found among some of the official control staff as regards their knowledge, particularly regarding certain aspects of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

In one of the establishments visited, for Listeria monocytogenes in products under point 1.2 of Chapter 1 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, the FBO used criterion "not detected in 25g" before the food left the premises. The OVs responsible for the regular official controls at this establishment stated that the applicable criterion for these products at retail level would be 100 cfu/g, although the FBO did not have any shelf-life studies (e.g. challenge tests) to prove that (see also paragraph 16).

In some of the establishments visited, the number of sample units the FBOs take for testing meat products against food safety criteria did not comply with the number of sampling units provided for in Chapter 1 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. One sample unit was taken instead of the required five. In other cases, 5 sample units were taken and then were pooled into one 125g sample in the laboratory. The results indicated absence in 25g (e.g. for Salmonella or Listeria) instead of absence in 125g. These cases were not detected during official controls. The representatives of the Länder CAs explained to the audit team that in their opinion, pooling of sample units in the frame of testing against the criteria laid down in Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 is permitted if there are studies on the particular food matrix and relevant microorganism combination that demonstrate equivalent results to individual tested sample units. This practice has to be approved by the CAs on the basis of evidence provided.

However, these controls are not effective to identify the systemic non-compliances in small-scale food business in relation to the arrangements regarding the design and implementation of FBOs' procedures based on HACCP principles. In addition, in the medium/large-scale food businesses there are some weaknesses in CAs' assessment of the adequacy of HACCP plans and, in particular, of FBOs' own check sampling plans.
